paras: The lynching of Joseph E. Jenkins and Eugene Azar took place in St. Martin Parish, Louisiana, in the night of 15-16 May 1882, when some 200 to 300 men took Jenkins from the parish jail at St. Martinsville and hanged him near Breaux Bridge, along with Azar, a Black man who was out on bail. Governor McEnery offered a $2,000 reward, and within weeks eleven to sixteen men were held in the parish jail. Later dispatches drew wider notice by calling Azar's hanging unjust and describing armed Black residents who swore vengeance.

According to the Lafayette Advertiser, on the night of Monday, 8 May, Jenkins shot and killed his brother-in-law, Raphael Castille, near Breaux Bridge. The paper said Jenkins had been lying in wait for a man named Mathieu, whom he had forbidden to enter his premises, and shot Castille by mistake. On an affidavit by the coroner, Dr. A. Guilbeau, Jenkins was arrested and jailed at St. Martinsville to await trial, and the St. Martinsville Observer declined to give details of the "sad affair."

Azar had earlier been charged with a killing, though reports disagreed on what he had done. A Baton Rouge special said an inquest had found the killing apparently in self-defence and that he had been let out on $300 bail.

A dispatch from Breaux Bridge dated 15 May said that about 300 men gathered there that day, went to St. Martinsville, and took Jenkins from the jail. They brought him back through Breaux Bridge, where he looked pale and was wrapped in a blanket, to the spot where Castille had been shot, and hanged him from a tree about half a mile from town. The Baton Rouge wire placed the attack on the jail early on the morning of the 16th and said Jenkins was taken out of his cell.

The same crowd seized Azar and hanged him from the same tree. The Times-Democrat said the men came across him on the way from St. Martinsville, while the Baton Rouge wire said they hunted him up afterward and hanged him despite his protests of innocence. A later special reported that Jenkins' hands had not been tied, that he grasped the rope, and that the crowd broke his arms with clubs before he strangled; his wife was said to have been among the spectators, begging for his life.

Governor McEnery telegraphed the sheriff that he had offered $2,000 for the arrest and conviction of those who hanged Jenkins and Azar. By 25 May sixteen of the mob were reported arrested, though the St. Martinsville Observer put the number at eleven. The Louisiana Sugar Bowl reported that the accused appeared before Judge Theodore Fontelieu at St. Martinsville for a two-day preliminary examination, after which he refused bail. In a decision dated 10 June in State vs. Placide Huval and others, Fontelieu ordered eleven named prisoners held without bail, writing that bail would make justice "a farce and a mockery." No report of a trial or its outcome was found.

Responses in the parish divided. A visitor told the St. Martinsville Observer that the lynchers had "the sympathy of the entire community" around Breaux Bridge. Baton Rouge specials of 25 May described a "reign of terror," with bands of armed Black men in St. Martinsville swearing vengeance for Azar and a "war of races" feared.

The story reached papers across the country through two wire versions on 17-18 May, a Times-Democrat special from St. Martinsville and a separate Baton Rouge dispatch, under heads such as "Lynched," "Double Lynching in Louisiana" and "Two Men Hanged by a Mob." These short items called Jenkins a "murderer" without qualification and said little of Azar beyond an alleged killing; reprints ran as far away as Idaho and Montana into mid-June.

The tone changed after the arrests. A New Orleans item headed "Arrested for Lynching the Wrong Man" said Azar had been out on bail for petty larceny, and a Times-Star special called his offence "so slight" and his hanging "unjust," while giving its headline to "Armed Negroes Swearing Vengeance." The San Antonio Evening Light condemned the hangings as "acts of gross murder" and said Louisiana could not claim a place among law-abiding states. Louisiana papers carried the local dispatch, the court proceedings and the Observer's note of community sympathy, mostly without comment.

Accounts of Azar differ in his name, printed as Azar, Azor, James Ascor and Ayrose, and in his alleged offence, given as killing a young man in January, murdering a young white man, petty larceny, or a fatal horse collision. The Baton Rouge wire called the mob "whites and blacks," while a later special called it a mob of "white men." Dates also vary: the local dispatch is dated 15 May and the Times-Democrat said Monday night, while other papers gave Tuesday, Wednesday or "the 16th." Only the Evening Light said the two men had been convicted and were awaiting execution; the local reports describe Jenkins as awaiting trial and Azar as out on bail.

accounts.label: Times-Democrat special from St. Martinsville
accounts.gist: Three hundred men took Jenkins from jail to the site of the murder near Breaux Bridge and hanged him; on the way they came across Azar, who had killed a young man in January, and hanged him on the same tree.

accounts.label: Baton Rouge wire
accounts.gist: A mob of whites and blacks attacked the jail early on the 16th, hanged Jenkins, then hunted up James Azor, out on bail on a charge of murdering a young white man, and hanged him despite his protests of innocence.

accounts.label: Breaux Bridge dispatch
accounts.gist: Dated May 15: about 300 men gathered at Breaux Bridge, took Jenkins from St. Martinsville, passed through Breaux Bridge, and hanged him half a mile from town with a Black man released on bond.

accounts.label: Later Baton Rouge specials
accounts.gist: A mob of white men hanged the Black man on a slight charge; Jenkins' arms were broken with clubs; armed Black residents swore vengeance and sixteen lynchers were jailed.

framing.detail: Most papers ran one- or two-sentence wire items under heads such as 'Lynched', 'Double Lynching in Louisiana' and 'Two Men Hanged by a Mob', calling Jenkins a 'murderer' outright.
The San Antonio Evening Light called the hangings 'acts of gross murder' and said Louisiana could not claim a place among law-abiding states.
Later dispatches headed 'Arrested for Lynching the Wrong Man' and 'A Reign of Terror. Armed Negroes Swearing Vengeance' called Azar's hanging unjust while framing the Black response as a threat.
Louisiana papers ran the local dispatch and court news, and the St. Martinsville Observer relayed that the lynchers had local sympathy.
